title: What is the difference between narrow dependencies (each parent partition used by at most one child — `map`, `filter`, no shuffle) and wide dependencies (one parent partition used by multiple children — `groupByKey`, `reduceByKey`, `join` — triggers a shuffle)?

s1_definition.profdef: Dependencies describe how a child RDD's partitions depend on its parent's partitions. A narrow dependency is one where each parent partition is used by at most one child partition, as with map, filter, and union, so computation can be pipelined within a single stage without moving data across the network. A wide dependency, also called a shuffle dependency, is one where a single parent partition contributes to multiple child partitions, as with groupByKey, reduceByKey, and join, which requires a shuffle that redistributes data across executors and creates a stage boundary.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine clerks at the National Bank of India each holding one box of transaction slips. A narrow operation is like "stamp every slip in your box as processed" — each clerk works entirely within their own box, no slips leave the desk, everyone finishes in parallel. A wide operation is like "re-sort every slip in the whole office so all of Rajesh's slips end up in one box and all of Priya's in another" — now slips must be carried between every desk, there is a big reshuffle, and everyone has to wait until the reshuffle finishes before the next step can start.
s1_definition.oneliner: Narrow dependencies keep each child partition fed by one parent partition with no shuffle, while wide dependencies spread one parent partition across many children and force an expensive network shuffle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Dependencies describe how a child RDD's partitions depend on its parent's partitions. A narrow dependency is one where each parent partition is used by at most one child partition, as with map, filter, and union, so computation can be pipelined within a single stage without moving data across the network. A wide dependency, also called a shuffle dependency, is one where a single parent partition contributes to multiple child partitions, as with groupByKey, reduceByKey, and join, which requires a shuffle that redistributes data across executors and creates a stage boundary.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine clerks at the National Bank of India each holding one box of transaction slips. A narrow operation is like "stamp every slip in your box as processed" — each clerk works entirely within their own box, no slips leave the desk, everyone finishes in parallel. A wide operation is like "re-sort every slip in the whole office so all of Rajesh's slips end up in one box and all of Priya's in another" — now slips must be carried between every desk, there is a big reshuffle, and everyone has to wait until the reshuffle finishes before the next step can start.

**One line to remember:** Narrow dependencies keep each child partition fed by one parent partition with no shuffle, while wide dependencies spread one parent partition across many children and force an expensive network shuffle.

sections.s2_technical:
A narrow dependency is the cheap, friendly kind. In operations like map, filter, flatMap, and mapPartitions, the records in a child partition come entirely from a single parent partition. Because of that, Spark can compute the whole chain of narrow operations within one task on one executor, pipelining them together so the data is read once and transformed in a single pass. There is no network movement and no waiting for other tasks. Spark groups consecutive narrow operations into the same stage precisely because they can run back-to-back without any data exchange.

A wide dependency is the expensive kind, and it is where shuffles come from. In operations like groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, distinct, and repartition, a child partition needs records from many parent partitions, because records must be grouped by key and the matching keys are scattered across all parent partitions. To bring them together, Spark performs a shuffle: each task writes its output to local disk bucketed by the target partition, and then the next stage's tasks read the relevant buckets from every previous task across the network. This is costly in disk input-output, network transfer, and serialization, and it forces a stage boundary because the second stage cannot start until all the first stage's shuffle writes are done.

The practical consequences are large. First, shuffles determine where stages break, so counting the wide dependencies in a job tells you how many stages it has. Second, shuffles are usually the dominant cost, so optimizing a Spark job is often a matter of reducing or cheapening shuffles. A classic example is preferring reduceByKey over groupByKey: reduceByKey combines values locally on each partition before the shuffle, so far less data crosses the network, whereas groupByKey ships every value and can cause memory problems. Another is using a broadcast join when one side is small, which avoids shuffling the large side entirely.

A senior nuance is that if two RDDs are already partitioned by the same key with the same partitioner, a join between them becomes a narrow dependency because matching keys are already co-located, so no shuffle is needed — this is the idea behind co-partitioning and bucketed tables. Also, data skew makes wide dependencies worse: if one key has far more records than others, its shuffle partition becomes a hotspot and one task runs long after the rest finish. In my banking jobs, recognizing which operations were wide and rewriting groupByKey into reduceByKey or pre-partitioning by account id was consistently the biggest performance win.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Stamping each transaction as processed can be done by each clerk within their own box. This is exactly a narrow dependency — no data movement.

Problem 2 — Totalling spending per account requires gathering all of one account's transactions, which are scattered across boxes. This is exactly a wide dependency — a shuffle.

Problem 3 — The bank wants to see that combining values locally before the shuffle (reduceByKey) moves far less data than shipping everything (groupByKey). This is exactly the key optimization for wide dependencies.

The mini-project models both. `NarrowOps.mapStamp` transforms each partition independently and reports zero records shuffled. `WideOps.groupByKey` shuffles every value across partitions and counts records moved, while `WideOps.reduceByKey` combines locally first and counts the much smaller number of records moved. The demo runs all three over Rajesh's and Priya's transactions and prints the shuffle volume so the difference is visible.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five transactions across two partitions — partition 0 has Rajesh Rs.1000, Priya Rs.500, Rajesh Rs.2000; partition 1 has Rajesh Rs.3000 and Priya Rs.700.

Step 1: The narrow map runs. Each partition is stamped in place, producing a stamped string per transaction. Each parent partition yields exactly one child partition and zero records move across the network.

Step 2: The wide groupByKey runs. To total per account, every single value must be routed to the partition that owns its key, so all five records cross the shuffle. The log warns that five records were shuffled.

Step 3: groupByKey produces totals of Rs.6000 for Rajesh and Rs.1200 for Priya, but at the cost of moving every value.

Step 4: The wide reduceByKey runs. On partition 0 it first combines locally into Rajesh Rs.3000 and Priya Rs.500; on partition 1 it combines into Rajesh Rs.3000 and Priya Rs.700. Only these four partials cross the shuffle.

Step 5: reduceByKey merges the partials into the same totals — Rajesh Rs.6000 and Priya Rs.1200 — but moved only four records instead of five, and the gap grows much larger with real volumes because each partition emits at most one partial per key.

Step 6: The journey shows the core lesson: narrow operations move nothing, wide operations move data, and map-side combine in reduceByKey makes a wide operation far cheaper than groupByKey.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] NARROW map: each partition processed in place — 0 records shuffled
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] WIDE groupByKey: shuffled 5 records across the network
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] groupByKey totals = {SAV2001=6000, CUR3001=1200}
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] WIDE reduceByKey: shuffled only 4 partial records (map-side combine)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] reduceByKey totals = {SAV2001=6000, CUR3001=1200}
```

```text

  NARROW (map stamp):
  P0 ──stamp in place──→ P0'        P1 ──stamp in place──→ P1'
  (1 parent → 1 child, 0 shuffled, same stage)

  WIDE groupByKey (ships every value):
  P0 ─┐                                    ┌─→ Part(SAV2001): R1000,R2000,R3000
      ├── SHUFFLE all 5 values across net ─┤
  P1 ─┘                                    └─→ Part(CUR3001): P500,P700
      (stage boundary: stage2 waits for stage1 shuffle writes)

  WIDE reduceByKey (map-side combine first):
  P0 local → {SAV:3000, CUR:500}  ─┐
                                   ├─ SHUFFLE only 4 partials ─→ merge → {SAV:6000, CUR:1200}
  P1 local → {SAV:3000, CUR:700}  ─┘
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The difference between narrow and wide dependencies is one of the most important things to understand in Spark because it explains both how jobs are divided into stages and where the cost goes. A narrow dependency is one where each parent partition is used by at most one child partition, which is the case for operations like map, filter, and flatMap. Because each child partition's data comes entirely from a single parent partition, Spark can pipeline a whole chain of narrow operations inside one task on one executor, reading the data once and transforming it in a single pass with no network movement. That is why consecutive narrow operations are grouped into the same stage.

A wide dependency, also called a shuffle dependency, is one where a single parent partition contributes to many child partitions, which happens with groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, distinct, and repartition. To group records by key, Spark must bring matching keys together, and since they are scattered across all parent partitions, it performs a shuffle: every task writes its output to local disk bucketed by target partition, and the next stage reads the relevant buckets from every task across the network. This is expensive in disk, network, and serialization, and it forces a stage boundary because the downstream stage cannot begin until all shuffle writes finish. So the number of wide dependencies in a job equals the number of shuffle boundaries, which equals the number of stages beyond the first.

In my project at the National Bank of India, reducing and cheapening shuffles was consistently the biggest performance lever. The clearest example was replacing groupByKey with reduceByKey when totalling spending per account: reduceByKey combines values locally on each partition before the shuffle, so only one partial per key per partition crosses the network instead of every single value, which both runs faster and avoids memory blowups. I also pre-partitioned transaction data by account id so that joins on account id became narrow and needed no shuffle at all, and I watched for data skew, where one hot key makes a single shuffle task run long after the others finish. Recognizing which operations are wide, and designing to avoid or shrink those shuffles, is how I made our banking pipelines fast.
